title: The Clean Air Act of 1970 and Adult Mortality
research_question: Does a sustained reduction in ambient total suspended particulates (TSPs) air pollution lead to lower mortality rates among adults and the elderly? Specifically, what is the effect of long-run, regulation-induced declines in particulate concentrations on annual death rates of people over age 50 and those aged 65–84?
data_description: The analysis uses county-level annual data for 1969–1974 covering approximately 501 U.S. counties with consistent pollution monitoring (representing over 60% of the U.S. population aged 50+). Mortality data come from the National Center for Health Statistics Mortality Detail files, providing a near-census of deaths by age, race, gender, cause, and county of residence; these are aggregated into county-by-age-by-race-by-gender cells. Population denominators come from the National Cancer Institute SEER database and U.S. Census Bureau intercensal estimates. Annual mean TSPs concentrations and counts of daily exceedances are constructed from EPA monitor-level data obtained via FOIA. County-level economic covariates—per-capita income, earnings, employment shares (including manufacturing), transfer payments, income maintenance, family assistance, and medical expenditures—are drawn from the Bureau of Economic Analysis and the Regional Economic Information System.
institutional_context: The 1970 Clean Air Act Amendments established National Ambient Air Quality Standards for six pollutants, including total suspended particulates. Beginning in 1972, the EPA classified each U.S. county as either 'attainment' or 'nonattainment' for TSPs based on whether 1970 pollution readings exceeded federal ceilings: an annual geometric mean above 75 µg/m³ or a second-highest daily concentration above 260 µg/m³. Counties designated nonattainment were subject to substantially stricter regulation of local industrial and fuel-combustion emission sources, with the goal of bringing all counties into compliance by 1975 (extendable to 1977). This federally mandated, threshold-based assignment generated sharp differences across otherwise similar counties in the regulatory pressure to abate particulate emissions, producing markedly larger TSPs declines in nonattainment counties beginning in 1972.
